Herbert Bayer, Research in Development of Universal Type

Bayer’s single-case alphabet drawn from arcs and straight strokes, the reference point for Bauhaus lowercase typography.

Source
Harvard Art Museums: Research in Development of Universal Type (BR48.94)
Creator
Herbert Bayer
Made
1927 (Harvard’s date for this drawing)
Style
Bauhaus (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Rational, geometric, systematic
Evidence
Based on the Harvard Art Museums record and the Bauhaus Kooperation workshop page. The museum image did not download (HTTP 403), so no image of the drawing was inspected. A digital “universal” specimen on Commons was not used because it is a modern revival, not Bayer’s drawing.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

No image is stored. The drawing is still in copyright (© Artists Rights Society / VG Bild-Kunst).

Context

Harvard dates the drawing 1927 and describes it as black ink and gouache on cream wove paper, 37.5 × 60.4 cm. Bayer gave it to the Busch-Reisinger Museum in 1948. Harvard BR48.94.

Graphite notes in Bayer’s hand read “abbildung 1. alfabet. g und k ist noch als unfertig zu betrachten” (figure 1, alphabet; g and k are to be considered unfinished) and “beispiel eines zeichnens in grösserem massta[b] präcise optische wirkung.” Harvard BR48.94.

Bauhaus Kooperation says Bayer based his type design on the simplest geometric elements, with the goal of standardizing communication and a uniform typographic identity for the Bauhaus; the workshop’s type reform was most visible in the use of lowercase only. Bauhaus Kooperation: Druck und Reklame.

Bayer led the Dessau printing and advertising workshop from 1925 to 1928. Bauhaus Kooperation: Herbert Bayer.

Why it belongs

The universal alphabet is more a program than a working typeface: one case, a few construction elements, and no historical ornament. It explains why lowercase headings read as “Bauhaus”.

Borrow

Set headings in lowercase only, in a geometric sans-serif with circular bowls.

Treat a type system as a small kit of arcs and straight strokes, and keep it consistent across all printed matter.
